messages.subject: LGCP in INLA vs inlabru
parts:
Hi all,

I have been fitting a LGCP model with a SPDE defining the spatial random effect and a mixture of linear and non-linear spatial covariates. 

When I fit the model in inlabru, I use a SpatialPointsDF for the coordinates and a rasterization of my covariates in a SpatialPixelsDF format. The trouble is, the effect of the SPDE is null (the overall intensity plot looks reasonable as do the covariate effects) but it has an obvious pattern when included in the model on its own. I have tried different meshes and variations in the prior parameters with no luck. Is this because the spatial covariates are capturing all of the underlying pattern? (I struggle to believe this is the case as I have rasterized the covariates and lost some resolution in doing so).

When I fit the model in INLA, I keep my data in its original format (SpatialPolygonsDF) and model the count ~ covariates + SPDE (with the weights defined as the area of each polygon), getting a nice intensity value per polygon as a result. The outputs here (mean intensity, effect of spatial field, and covariate effects) all look good/reasonable. 

I am wondering as to the difference - and why the effect of my spatial random field might be nullified when using inlabru.

And also if it would be possible to keep the SpatialPolygonsDF of covariates when fitting the LGCP in inlabru.

Finally - in terms of residual analysis; I followed the vignette Residual Analysis of spatial point process models using Bayesian methods • inlabru (inlabru-org.github.io) for my inlabru LGCP. If I wanted to do this for my INLA LGCP (as this seems to produce the desired spatial random field pattern), are there methods/functions in place that translate this vignette for INLA models? Or would it be a manual job?

Apologies for the lengthy post, any help is greatly appreciated!

Thanks,
Erin

messages.author: afb003e064114795
messages.subject: Re: [r-inla] LGCP in INLA vs inlabru
parts:
Hi Erin,

from 2.9.0 (and 2.8.0, but with some automation issues) inlabru
handles polygon based covariates via the eval_spatial() methods; if
you supply a SPolygonsDF or an sf object with polygons, it will call
eval_spatial() to extract the covariates, so you don't need to
pre-rasterize them.

Have you tried running the count based model in inlabru as well, to
check if there's some inlabru specific issue also with that one? For
example, the default intercept prior is different in plain inla and in
inlabru, as in inlabru it's treated the same as other covariates, and
this can change the estimates a bit. However, I wouldn't expect it to
suppress the spde component, so that's probably not the issue.
What are the paraterm estimates? How close to zero is the estimated
spde standard deviation? (sigma in the pcmatern model). Also check
that your priors are sensible (in particular the range and sigma
parameters), taking note that sigma is the std.dev. for the Gaussian
field, and it's applied in an exponential link context, so large
values quickly become too large.

Finn

matern  <- inla.spde2.pcmatern(mesh_fine, prior.sigma = c(0.1, 0.01), prior.range = c(1, 0.01))

  data.frame(x = locations$x, y = locations$y),

)
Jdf$count <- as.numeric(Japan$LandslideC) 
^ dataframe holding geometry and response variable

cmp <- count ~ Intercept(1) + field(geometry, matern)

fit <- bru(cmp, Jdf, family = "gaussian") 
^I used "gaussian" for simplicity as I was just trying to run the model fit without getting the error

Thanks,
Erin

parts:
Hi,

I found the reason:
cmp <- count ~ Intercept(1) + field(geometry, matern)

should be

cmp <- count ~ Intercept(1) + field(geometry, model = matern)

You can see in the help text for the component constructor,
?component, that the model parameter "model" comes after "...". This
in R means that you have to name it explicitly.
Also, if it _had_ come before "...", it still wouldn't have been the
second argument (which is "weights", just like in ordinary INLA::f()
calls).

The cryptic error message came from inlabru attempting to compute the
derivative of the "product between the weights object and the latent
state", which is clearly undefined when "weights" has accidentally
become a "matern" model object. I'm actually amazed that it got that
far in the code before trying to do something invalid with that object
without noticing.

Finn

I've now added some extra checks to the inlabru code to detect invalid
mapper inputs sooner and give more informative messages when it does;
the logic that lead to your specific error message is still a bit
non-intuitive, as it's not the inadvertent invalid "weights" input
that's detected, but rather that the lack of a model specification
lead to it defaulting to model="linear", which in turn makes the
main=geometry input invalid for the bru_mapper_linear() mapping!
The extra checks&messages are in inlabru from 2.9.0.9013, see
https://inlabru-org.github.io/inlabru/news/index.html

Finn

On Thursday, September 21, 2023 at 4:58:43 PM UTC+1 Finn Lindgren wrote:
Hi,

I found the reason:

cmp <- count ~ Intercept(1) + field(geometry, matern)

should be

cmp <- count ~ Intercept(1) + field(geometry, model = matern)

You can see in the help text for the component constructor,
?component, that the model parameter "model" comes after "...". This
in R means that you have to name it explicitly.
Also, if it _had_ come before "...", it still wouldn't have been the
second argument (which is "weights", just like in ordinary INLA::f()
calls).

The cryptic error message came from inlabru attempting to compute the
derivative of the "product between the weights object and the latent
state", which is clearly undefined when "weights" has accidentally
become a "matern" model object. I'm actually amazed that it got that
far in the code before trying to do something invalid with that object
without noticing.

Finn

Progress!

Check all your crs info's; fm_crs(mesh), fm_crs(Jdf), etc, etc. and
